claims.claimed: He sets out two camps. Transhumanists hold that technologies for enhancing people should be widely available and that individuals should have broad freedom to use them on themselves; their opponents, whom he calls bioconservatives, want broad bans because they think enhancement would undermine human dignity. He writes that enhancements may possibly make us or our descendants what he calls posthuman: beings with indefinitely long healthy lives, much greater intellectual abilities and control of their own emotions. claims.claimed: By an upload they mean a creature whose thoughts and sensations have been moved from a brain to computer hardware. They argue that a person who uploads in order to go on living is probably dying instead, and that what comes out is at best a psychological duplicate. claims.claimed: Questions that used to belong to philosophy, he says, are moving to engineering, and engineers and their investors will not wait. claims.claimed: The paper estimates that human behaviour carries information at about 10 bits a second across the tasks it examines (typing, speaking, memory contests and others), while the senses gather about a billion, and it says the gap is unexplained. In the section on Musk it calls the feeling that our inner life is much richer than we can express "the Musk illusion", quotes Musk saying Neuralink's purpose is a high-bandwidth interface "such that we can be symbiotic with AI" because "we have a bandwidth problem", and predicts that Musk's brain, linked to a computer, would communicate at about 10 bits a second; a telephone, it says, would do as well. The next section, on brain-computer interfaces for patients, says such devices "could greatly benefit" people who struggle to speak, and that "one really needs to convey only a few bits per second to and from the brain". Hedges: the authors call the cause of the limit an open question and propose research to explain it; the prediction about Musk rests on the research they review, not on a measurement of an implant.
